Yes. With the natural correction
\[
\alpha_*:=\sup_{n\ge1}\tau_n^{1/n}
\]
to the parenthetical formula in the question, one has \(\alpha_*=\sqrt6\).

**Theorem.** For every integer \(n\ge1\),
\[
\tau_n\le(\sqrt6)^n.
\]
Consequently, the smallest \(\alpha>0\) such that \(\tau_n\le\alpha^n\) for every \(n\) is \(\sqrt6\).

**Proof.** For \(n\ge2\), let
\[
c_n:=
\frac{\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/6}\sin^{n-2}t\,dt}
     {\displaystyle\int_0^\pi\sin^{n-2}t\,dt}.
\]
This is the normalized surface area of a spherical cap of angular radius \(\pi/6\) in \(S^{n-1}\). The contact points of a kissing configuration have pairwise angular distance at least \(\pi/3\). Hence the caps of angular radius \(\pi/6\) centered at them have disjoint interiors, and therefore
\[
\tau_n c_n\le1. \tag{1}
\]
We shall prove
\[
c_n\ge6^{-n/2} \tag{2}
\]
for every \(n\ge2\), except for \(n=3\), which will be handled separately.

Put
\[
I_m:=\int_0^{\pi/6}\sin^m t\,dt,
\qquad
J_m:=\int_0^\pi\sin^m t\,dt,
\]
so that \(c_n=I_m/J_m\) for \(m=n-2\). Integration by parts gives
\[
I_{m+2}
 =\frac{m+1}{m+2}I_m
  -\frac{\sqrt3}{(m+2)2^{m+2}},
\qquad
J_{m+2}=\frac{m+1}{m+2}J_m.
\]
Consequently,
\[
c_{n+2}
 =c_n-\frac{\sqrt3}{(m+1)2^{m+2}J_m}. \tag{3}
\]

By concavity of \(\sin\) on \([0,\pi]\), its graph on \([0,\pi/6]\) lies above the chord joining its endpoints. Thus
\[
\sin t\ge\frac{3t}{\pi}
\qquad(0\le t\le\pi/6).
\]
It follows that
\[
I_m\ge\int_0^{\pi/6}\left(\frac{3t}{\pi}\right)^m dt
    =\frac{\pi}{6(m+1)2^m}.
\]
Moreover,
\[
\frac{\pi}{6}>\frac{3\sqrt3}{10};
\]
for example, \(\pi>157/50\) and \(\sqrt3<26/15\) give
\[
\frac{\pi}{6}>\frac{157}{300}>
\frac{13}{25}>\frac{3\sqrt3}{10}.
\]
Hence
\[
I_m>
\frac{3\sqrt3}{10(m+1)2^m}. \tag{4}
\]
Combining (3) and (4), and using \(J_m>0\), gives
\[
\frac{\sqrt3}{(m+1)2^{m+2}J_m}
 <\frac56\frac{I_m}{J_m}
 =\frac56c_n.
\]
Therefore
\[
c_{n+2}>\frac{c_n}{6}. \tag{5}
\]

Now \(c_2=1/6\), so (5) proves (2) in every even dimension. Also, direct integration gives
\[
c_5=\frac12-\frac{9\sqrt3}{32}.
\]
Since \(\sqrt3<26/15\), we have \(c_5>1/80\). On the other hand,
\[
(\sqrt6)^5=36\sqrt6>80
\]
because \(\sqrt6>20/9\). Thus \(c_5>6^{-5/2}\), and (5) proves (2) in every odd dimension \(n\ge5\).

It remains to treat dimensions \(1\) and \(3\). Clearly
\[
\tau_1=2<\sqrt6.
\]
For \(n=3\),
\[
c_3=\frac{2-\sqrt3}{4}>\frac1{15},
\]
again because \(\sqrt3<26/15\). By (1), \(\tau_3<15\), and hence \(\tau_3\le14\). Finally,
\[
14<6\sqrt6=(\sqrt6)^3,
\]
since \(\sqrt6>7/3\). This proves \(\tau_n\le(\sqrt6)^n\) for every \(n\ge1\).

The constant is optimal: \(\tau_2=6\), so every universal base \(\alpha\) must satisfy \(6\le\alpha^2\), and therefore \(\alpha\ge\sqrt6\). \(\square\)
